messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

María was twenty-two when she fled her home in Central America, leaving behind a country that had become a battlefield. She had been a university student, studying social work, when soldiers came to her campus one afternoon. They rounded up students in the courtyard, shouting orders in Spanish that cracked through the air like whips. María remembered the smell of alcohol on the breath of the commanding officer as he leaned close to her face, the way his uniform seemed to fill her entire field of vision, and the sound of his voice—sharp, absolute, leaving no room for refusal. She had done exactly what she was told, standing frozen while they searched the dormitories, and later that night, she fled across the border with nothing but the clothes on her back. Now, twelve years later, she worked as a prison guard in a state correctional facility, a job she had taken because it offered stability and a steady paycheck for her family. But every shift brought her back to that courtyard.

The triggers were everywhere, though she had not always recognized them. When she walked into the prison’s common area and caught the sour scent of alcohol on an inmate’s breath, her chest would tighten before she even understood why. When a supervisor gave her a direct order—even a routine one, like “lock down cell block C”—she felt her throat close, a wave of heat rising through her body. And whenever she saw a corrections officer in full uniform, especially one with a stern expression, she had to fight the urge to look away, to shrink. These moments did not just pass; they activated something inside her. The smell of alcohol, the sound of an order, the sight of a uniform—each one told her, with the force of a physical blow, that the world was still dangerous, that people in authority could not be trusted, that she was no longer the person she had been before that afternoon. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, that people were not what they seemed, and that somewhere along the way, she had lost herself entirely. And because she believed this, she began to scan for danger constantly—a flicker of movement in her peripheral vision made her flinch, and she would find herself reacting as if she were under threat even in the prison’s quiet hallways, her heart hammering for no reason she could name. She always chose her seat in the break room with her back to the wall, facing the door, so she could see anyone approaching.

The memories themselves were relentless. They came back to her with startling clarity—the exact shade of the officer’s uniform, the texture of the concrete beneath her feet, and, most disturbingly, the sounds: the scrape of boots, the metallic click of a radio, the officer’s voice repeating commands. When the memory returned, it overwhelmed her completely, forcing her to stop whatever she was doing, her hands trembling, her vision blurring. These vivid, detailed recollections reinforced everything she already feared. They proved to her that the world was dangerous, that she could not trust anyone, that she had been fundamentally changed. And so she tried to push them away. She would put on loud music or television at home, drowning out the silence that might invite the memories back. She would dwell on how the event could have been prevented—if only she had stayed in her dorm room, if only she had run sooner—as if by replaying it she could rewrite it. She avoided being around people in authority or uniform outside of work, turning down invitations to social gatherings where she might encounter police officers or military veterans. But these strategies only made things worse. The rumination kept the memory fresh and painful, confirming her belief that she was weak, that she had failed. The sensory distraction allowed the memory to surface the moment the music stopped, catching her off guard. And when she avoided authority figures, she felt a surge of relief that only reinforced her sense that they were dangerous. She began to notice authority figures everywhere—in the grocery store, at her daughter’s school, on the news—so that even outside the prison, she could not escape.

The cycle tightened over months and years. A trigger—the smell of alcohol on an inmate’s breath—would activate her belief that the world was dangerous, which made her hypervigilant, scanning for threat, which in turn brought back the memory of the officer’s voice, which overwhelmed her and made her feel even more unsafe. She would then put on loud music in her car to block it out, which prevented her from processing the memory, leaving it raw and ready to be triggered again the next day. At work, she had started avoiding certain corridors where the smell of cleaning alcohol lingered, and she had asked for a transfer to a less busy post, which her supervisor granted but not without a comment about her performance. Her husband noticed she was distant, that she flinched when he touched her shoulder unexpectedly, that she spent her evenings in front of the television with the volume turned up, not speaking. She had come to believe that she did not know herself anymore, that the woman who had once dreamed of becoming a social worker was gone, replaced by someone who jumped at shadows and scanned every room for exits.

What finally brought María to seek help was a moment in the prison cafeteria. A new officer, a young man with a clean uniform and a commanding voice, had walked past her table and said, “Guard, I need you on the east wing in five.” The words were routine, but the tone—the authority, the expectation of immediate compliance—sent her reeling. She had excused herself, locked herself in a bathroom stall, and sat on the floor, her hands over her ears, the memory of the officer’s breath and voice so vivid she could almost smell the alcohol again. She stayed there for twenty minutes, trembling, unable to stop the tears. That evening, she told her husband she needed help. She was afraid of what would happen if she did not—afraid she would lose her job, afraid she would lose herself completely, afraid that the world she had tried so hard to escape had followed her here, and that it would never let her go.
